column5: GHA VII (Chanaiwa, tail of the Southern Africa chapter, 1985): Herero revolt in 01/1904 killed 100 Germans; von Trotha sought total destruction; 75 to 80 per cent of an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero were slaughtered, 14,000 put in prison camps, 2,000 fled to South Africa. This is a range with a loose method and no Nama figure; the course's 80,000 to under 20,000 (Hochschild) and 'about 80 per cent' sit inside it, and the Nama toll must come from elsewhere [ESTIMATE]

GHA VII on the Ndebele-Shona Chimurenga 1896-97: 130 whites killed in Matabeleland in a week; toll estimated at 450 European dead and 188 wounded and 8,000 African deaths; spirit mediums (svikiro: Mukwati, Kagubi, Nehanda) gave the rising unity; Nehanda and Kagubi hanged after 02/03/1898 (the chapter says charged 02/03/1898); Rhodes negotiated with Ndebele indunas to 05/01/1898; Chimurenga continued in Mashonaland to 1903. The chapter rejects reading it as merely atavistic

GHA VII (Akpan) gives Adwa: Menelik over 100,000 men with modern rifles; Italians about 17,000 of whom 10,596 Italian, 56 guns to Menelik's 40; dead 261 officers, 2,918 other Italian ranks, about 2,000 askaris, 954 missing, 470 Italians and 958 askaris wounded; over 40 per cent casualties; 11,000 rifles lost; Peace of Addis Ababa 26/10/1896. These figures are Berkeley's (1902, cited in the chapter), the same chain as the course's worked example, so GHA VII is not an independent check

GHA VII on Wuchale: signed 02/05/1889; Article XVII differed in the Amharic and Italian texts (optional versus obligatory use of Italy for foreign contacts); Menelik denounced the treaty on 12/02/1893 with 82,000 rifles and 28 cannon; Menelik's reply 'Ethiopia has need of no one'. Confirms the course's Wuchale line; Italy occupied Adowa in 01/1890

GHA VII on Liberia: Liberia lost territory to Britain (1882, 1885, Kanre-Lahun 1911 with 4,000 pounds) and France (1891-92, 1907); never invited to Berlin; Americo-Liberian rule over indigenous groups was called colonial in nature by presidents Barclay and Tubman; Liberia and Ethiopia survived but were 'mutilated'; Menelik also expanded Ethiopia over lowland peoples, so independence did not mean no empire

GHA VII (Ranger, ch 3): resistance was general but varied in intensity (so compare regions); resistance by stateless societies (Igbo, Baule, Agni) was often longer-lived than that of states, whose rulers often lacked legitimacy (Samori, Shehu Ahmadu); some resistance targeted African authoritarianism as much as colonial rule, so 'nationalism' is a poor label (Steinhart); Ranger concedes his own account of 1896 Shona spirit mediums is disputed by Cobbing and Beach

GHA VII on Maji Maji: broke out in 1905 among the Matumbi of eastern Tanganyika, powered by a prophetic message from hinterland cult centres (Kinjikitile) plus populist Islam; after the coastal resistances of 1888-91 failed, the basis of protest widened; later prophets led witchcraft-eradication movements. Ranger gives no toll; the course's toll must stay with its own sources. Also Maherero's 1904 appeal: 'Let the whole of Africa fight against the Germans'

GHA VII (Boahen, ch 2 tail): why Europe won: quinine, knowledge of the interior, finance, African disunity, no European war over Africa to 1914, the Brussels Convention of 1890 on arms sales, Maxim and Gatling guns; only Samori and Menelik obtained modern weapons; about 30 per cent of borders are straight lines; about forty units by 1914; the partition was 'illegal and immoral' but returning to fluid pre-1879 borders would be dangerous. Wuchale: Italy claimed a protectorate; Adwa a defeat; Italy kept Eritrea and Somalia and took Libya in 1911

GHA VII (West Africa chapter tail) says the Baule population fell from about 1.5 million in 1900 to about 260,000 by 1911 after French suppression; this is an extreme figure from one source (Suret-Canale) and should not be repeated without a method [CONTESTED]. Same chapter: Yaa Asantewaa war 1900 over the Golden Stool and 4 shillings tax; Hut Tax war 1898; Brussels Convention banned arms sales; mass migration as protest; first Lagos strike 1897

GHA VII (Rodney, ch 14): the colonial economy rested on coercion more than capital: taxes (hut then poll), forced labour (French prestation until 1944; Congo rubber tax), pass laws in South Africa and German South West Africa, and floggings by judicial order; foreign capital was small outside South Africa and Algeria; African peasants, not plantations, drove West African cash-crop exports (cocoa, groundnuts) and Africans fought colonial rules to plant better crops (Arabica coffee in Tanganyika); mining drew labour across Southern Africa; wages were kept low by work-cards

GHA VII (Rodney) is an argument as well as a record: it calls the Anglo-Boer war 'anti-imperialist in a perverse sense', treats the colonial economy as laid down by about 1935, and says colonial administration unintentionally prepared the elite and administrative frame of independence ('Westminster system' smoothest, Algeria and Portuguese Africa most radical). Rodney and Ranger wrote these chapters in the 1970s; label them as such

GHA VII (Mwanzi, East Africa chapter) rejects the heroes-and-villains split of resisters and collaborators (Boahen: see events as diplomacy, with or without force); examples: Waiyaki, Lenana, King Mumia's alliance with Britain, Nandi resistance until the leader was killed in 1905, Hehe under Mkwawa killed about 290 Germans in 1891, Abushiri hanged 15/12/1889, Kabarega and Mwanga captured 1899 and exiled to the Seychelles/Kismayu; people changed tactics over time

Boahen argues c.80% of Africa was still under African rule in 1880, and that the 1890-1910 conquest followed years of treaty-making in which Europeans first treated African rulers as equals; most rulers chose to defend sovereignty, differing only in strategy (diplomacy, war, alliance).

Boahen's introduction attacks the label 'collaborator' for African rulers who allied with Europeans (Tofa of Porto Novo, Lat Dior, Wobogo, Samori), calling it Eurocentric and inaccurate; he periodises 1880-1919 sovereignty defence, 1919-35 accommodation and protest, and 1935 Ethiopia as the break. Supports the course's existing remark that resist/collaborate is too simple.

Uzoigwe dates the Scramble from 1876-80 (Leopold, Portugal, French moves) rather than the 1882 Egypt occupation; says Berlin Act Articles 34-35 set notification and effective occupation, and that Berlin did not partition Africa only in the narrowest sense; political treaties were often fraudulent (Lugard himself called some utter fraud, Mwanga treaties imposed not negotiated).

Conquest summary lists French and British campaigns (Lat Dior d.1886, Samori captured 1898, Prempeh exiled, Jaja tricked 1887, Sudan 1898 with over 20 000 Sudanese dead). The chapter text in the file stops at p. 37 of 44, so the rest of the conquest summary is not in the copy. Slips: Wahehe dated 1889-8 and Rabih called 'of Sennar'.

Omdurman toll: Ibrahim gives nearly 11 000 Sudanese killed and about 16 000 wounded at Karari (2/9/1898); Uzoigwe in Chapter 2 says over 20 000 Sudanese died (Sudan reconquest in general). The course's 'at least 10,800' sits with Ibrahim; the two chapters differ and neither is a count of the one battle only.

Egypt: Urabi revolt began Feb 1881 with army grievances over Turco-Circassian monopoly of senior ranks; Alexandria bombarded 11/07/1882; Tel el-Kebir 13/09/1882; occupation lasted 72 years. Urabi's mistakes included not deposing Tawfik and not blocking the Suez Canal.

Egyptian nationalism before 1914: Mustafa Kamil and Dinshaway (1906) pushed Britain to change line; Umma Party cooperative; movement elitist and disunited. Mahdist state's insistence that Menelik accept Mahdism blocked an Ethiopia-Sudan alliance against Europe; Mahdist risings of 1900-14 identified British with the dajjal.

Libya under Italy: Cyrenaica resistance under Umar al-Mukhtar until his execution on 16/09/1931; Italians fenced the border, emptied the countryside into camps, with 'more than a hundred thousand' deaths reported and 30 000 of 80 000 dead in al-Brayqa 1930-32 on Italian figures; Badoglio declared conquest 24/01/1932. Course has no Libya material in M1 or M2.

Somali jihad under Sayyid Muhammad Abdule Hasan, 1899-1920: occupied Burao 1899, British expeditions 1900-04, Treaty of Illig 1905, destroyed the camel constabulary Aug 1913, died Nov 1920. Not in the course.

Laroui describes the colonial conquest sequence in North Africa (incident, anarchy claim, territorial pawn, delegated sovereignty by protectorate treaty, then 'pacification'), and argues resistance failed largely on numbers: Rif faced 300 000 French soldiers, Middle Atlas 10 000 people against 80 000 men. Also Tunisia treaty of 12/05/1881 and Moroccan Tuat loss 1899-1902.

West African conquest cases not in M1/M2: Lat Dior killed at Dekhle 27/10/1886 after opposing the Dakar-Saint-Louis railway; Ahmadu of the Tukulor allied with the French (Mango 1881, Gori 12/05/1887) before Archinard took Segu and Nioro 1890-91; Samori's army (30-35 000 sofa by 1887, Gras rifles copied by his blacksmiths, no artillery) fought the French to his capture 29/09/1898; Behanzin of Dahomey lost Abomey Nov 1892, arrested 29/01/1894.

Baule resistance (Etien Komenan, Kouame Die shot 02/1902, Akafou beaten to death 07/1902, Clozel halted operations Nov 1902); Asante: Prempeh refused protection 1891, was exiled to Seychelles; Jaja tricked aboard ship 1887; Benin sacked 1897; Northern Nigeria emirates fell 1900-03 to Maxim guns. Authors stress treaties and force combined by Britain, near-pure force by France.

Second phase 1900-14: revolts under traditional leaders (Mamadou Lamine 1885-87 against forced labour on Kayes-Niger railway and telegraph; Hut Tax rebellion 1898 against 5s/10s tax; Yaa Asantewaa 1900). Chapter file stops at p. 141 of 148, so the rest of the Hut Tax and Asantewaa accounts were not available.

Luluabourg garrison mutiny of 1895 in the Congo Free State: rebels controlled most of Kasai for more than six months before loyalist troops beat them (the chapter says 'a mutiny' of the army two years later too). Matches the course's Luluabourg line.

Central African strategies: Chokwe, Ovimbundu and Chikunda often better armed than Free State and Portuguese troops; Barue made powder and rifles; over 90% of the Portuguese force that took the Zambezi valley in 1902 were African levies; the authors say historians underplay hard-won successes (Humbe and Cuamato killed 300 of 500 in 1904; Chokwe fought the Force Publique for twenty years). Chapter 8 also names day-to-day resistance: tax flight (50 000 fled the Zambezi valley into Rhodesia and Nyasaland 1895-1907), and the 'social bandit' Mapondera 1892-1903.

column4: ch-009 Chapter 8 and Chapter 7 tail (Mazrui/Mwanza text), pp. 162-168, 181-186
column5: East and Central Africa after conquest: Mumbo cult 1913, Giriama revolt 1914, Acholi 1911, Maji Maji 1905-07 over the communal cotton scheme (28 days a year), settler land seizure of the Maasai 1904 and 1911; Free State had 'more than a dozen' revolts 1885-1905 in the lower and central Congo; Tete mutiny 1917; independent churches as protest. Text of Chapter 8 stops at p. 186 of 193.

Southern Africa: Chanaiwa sets out three models (confrontation: Zulu, Ndebele; protectorate or wardship: Sotho, Swazi, Tswana, Lozi; alliance by small tributaries). Anglo-Zulu war: Frere's ultimatum 11/12/1878, invasion 11/01/1879, Isandhlwana 22/01/1879 (1 600 invaders killed), Zululand split into thirteen chiefdoms. Ndebele: Moffat treaty 11/02/1888, Rudd Concession with unwritten verbal terms, Mashonaland occupied 12/09/1890, war of 1893, 280 000 cattle seized.

Bechuanaland and Swaziland: Tswana rulers Khama, Sebele and Bathoen went to London in 1895 and kept protectorate status instead of being absorbed by Rhodes's Company; Swaziland had 364 concessions by 1890 (352 confirmed), was pawned to the Transvaal in 1894 and became a British protectorate in 1903. Shows the 'small kingdoms survived as protectorates, strong ones were conquered' pattern.

Insurrections to 1918: more than twenty in Central Africa; royal families and spirit mediums led them (Chioco 1897, Barue 1917 which freed the Zambezi valley briefly until about 30 000 Nguni mercenaries intervened; Ikaya rebellion in the Congo to 1921; Chilembwe 1915). The course already notes the Chimurenga revival; Chilembwe is dated 1915 here, supporting the course's correction of Rodney.

Herero toll as the course already has it: January 1904 rising killed about 100 Germans; 75 to 80 per cent of an estimated 60 000-80 000 killed, 14 000 in camps, 2 000 fled to South Africa; Chimurenga toll about 450 Europeans and 8 000 Africans (new here; the course has no Chimurenga toll).

Madagascar: Merina kingdom recognised by Britain 1817 and France 1862; France's two wars (1883-85, 1894-95), treaty of 17/12/1885 read differently by each side, Antananarivo taken 30/09/1895; the Menalamba rising (from 11/1895) against Christian oligarchy and French; Galliani abolished the monarchy 28/02/1897 and extended fifty days' unpaid labour to all men 16-60. Not in the course.

WWI figures differ from the course's: Crowder gives over a million African soldiers and more than 2.5 million people in war work, over 150 000 soldier and carrier deaths, at least 45 000 carrier deaths in East Africa, 483 000 colonial soldiers in the French army (course says 450 000 sent to Europe), Belgians impressed up to 260 000 porters (matches the course), Diagne's 1918 recruiting drive got 63 378 against a 40 000 target. Another source in the course gives a million carriers, so the totals are sources' own estimates.

WWI effects: revolts across French West Africa (Borgu 1916) mostly against recruitment, protest migrations cost French West Africa about 62 000 subjects, Sanusi invasion of Egypt 11/1915 and Niger 12/1916, Tripolitanian Republic 16/11/1918, Chilembwe 01/1915 triggered by Nyasa casualties, Egyptian fellahin hit by requisition; Chapter text stops at p. 304 of 311.

column4: ch-013 Chapter 12 (Crowder), p. 283; ch-012 Chapter 11 tail, pp. 276-282
column5: Liberia and Ethiopia survived through belief in destiny, diplomacy, great-power rivalry (1906 secret tripartite convention to divide Ethiopia) and, for Ethiopia only, arms: about 600 000 troops at the 1902 Adwa parade (disputed), Liberia a militia under 2 000 and debts that invited gunboat diplomacy. Menelik built Addis Ababa, the Djibouti railway concession 1894, Bank of Abyssinia 1905.
Congo chefferies cut from 6 095 in 1917 to 1 212 in 1938 (Franck reforms), as the course has it; French West Africa made cantons; British warrant chiefs in the east of Nigeria.

Indirect rule: Lugard's 1906 instructions made the emir a partner with the Resident advisory, but van Vollenhoven (1917) said the cercle commandant alone commands and the chief is an instrument; French 'association' worked only in Morocco under Lyautey. Betts argues the chief became an administrative agent everywhere, so the French/British contrast was one of procedure more than effect.

column4: ch-014 Chapter 13 (Betts) and ch-013 tail (Crowder), pp. 305-309, 323-324
column5: After 1918: Wilson's Fourteen Points and the mandate idea of 'sacred trust' raised demands; Diagne was promised reforms that were never put into effect; Kenyan settlers won a Legislative Council majority and the Crown Lands Ordinance; SANNC sent a memorandum to George V which never reached Versailles; Germany lost its colonies and the Ewe were split. Chapter text stops at p. 324 of 331 (justice section only).

Labour in French, Belgian and Portuguese Africa 1914-35: unpaid service raised from seven to twelve (AOF) or fifteen (AEF) days; 127 250 men recruited for the Congo-Ocean railway 1921-32 with probably some 20 000 deaths before 1928; Mozambique miners to the Rand 1913-30 averaged 50 000 a year (900 000 total, 35 000 died); Mozambique Company held sovereign powers to 1930. Course has none of this.

Depression 1930-35: Belgian Congo debt instalment 88% of 1933 revenue, exports fell by almost two-thirds 1930-33; head tax fell little (AOF 156 to 153 million francs 1929-35) while producer prices collapsed; peasants grew more cash crops to pay tax (AOF coffee 5 300 to 43 500 t in a year, cocoa 6 700 to 49 700 t, 1935-36); wartime requisition and famine in AEF/AOF (250 000-300 000 dead, Fang halved 140 000 to 65 000 by 1933); Niger 1930-31 famine with some mortality over 50%.

column4: ch-015 Chapter 14 (Rodney) tail and ch-016 first pages, pp. 344-349
column5: Rodney/Coquery-Vidrovitch argue the 'dual economy' idea misleads: the modern export sector took value from the village economy, and 1930-34 showed dependence (wage labour fell 50% or more, Gold Coast cocoa hold-ups 1920-21, 1930, 1938). Chapter text stops at p. 374 of 381.

Southern Rhodesia Land Apportionment Act (enacted 1930, enforced 04/1931) gave the European Area 50.8% and Native Reserves 22.4%, consistent with the course's line that settlers held over half the land by 1934. Kaniki says Europeans already held 12.5 million ha by 1925.

Kenya settler economy: alienated land rose from about 2 000 ha (1903) to 260 000 (1914) and 2.74 million ha (1930); Crown Lands Ordinance 1915 extended leases from 99 to 999 years; 64.8% of European land unproductive by 1930; Kenya governor in 1913 said taxation was the only way to compel Africans to seek work; kipande pass from 07/1920; Africans barred from coffee; African share of Kenya domestic exports fell from 24% (1913) to 9% (1932) while Europeans rose from 5% to 76%. West Africa differed: Aborigines' Rights Protection Society defeated the 1898 Lands Bill.

Minerals and marketing in British Africa: colonial administrations excluded Africans from diamonds (CAST, Sierra Leone Selection Trust 99-year monopoly from 1933); mining licence required reading the 1927 ordinance in English; Gold Coast cocoa hold-ups 10-12/1930 and 1937-38, broken by fines and jailing of chiefs; UAC handled nearly half West Africa's overseas trade in the 1930s; Imperial Preference 1932 and 100% tariff on non-British goods 1934.

Kaniki says the 1913 Natives' Land Act reserved 88% of South Africa for whites and 12% for reserves, but a page later gives 6 million Africans on reserves of 88 000 sq km against 1.14 million sq km for 1.8 million Europeans (about 7%). The course and the TRC use about 7% in 1913 (13.7% after 1936), so treat Kaniki's 12% as a slip or a later-figure blend; the 88 000 sq km figure fits the 7%.

South Africa 1880-1935: white miner earned eleven times an African miner in 1935; mines employed 163 000 in 1906 including 51 000 indentured Chinese; Civilised Labour Policy 1924; 1923 Urban Areas Act; reserve overpopulation and migrant 'men of two worlds'. Adds the labour-law chain around the 1913 Act that the course already treats.

column4: ch-018 Chapter 17 (Kassab; Abdussalam and Abusedra), pp. 421-446
column5: North African colonial economy: Algeria 25 795 settler estates covering 2.334 million ha in 1930; 1.1% of Muslim owners held 21% of Muslim land; Tunisia settler estates 700 000 ha in 1931; Moroccan phosphate exports 8 232 t (1921) to 1.179 million t (1930); Algerian wine price fell 168 to 54 francs (1927-34); Libya: Italian settlement cost about 800 million (lire/units unclear) for 85 000 settlers by 1936, sheep fell from 800 000 (1926) to 98 000 (1933), camels 75 000 to 2 000. Not in the course.

Caldwell warns that pre-1935 African population estimates (Willcox, Carr-Saunders, Durand) rest on little evidence: Willcox reused a 17th-century guess of 100 million; Durand's 1850 range was 81-145 million (about 30% error); sub-Saharan Africa passed 150 million by 1935. Useful caution for any population claim in the Congo or Maji Maji material.

Caldwell's slave-trade count: Curtin's 9.5 million to the Americas (UNESCO 1978 experts thought 15-30 million), with a net demographic deficit of about 4 million by 1880 (15% in the main source area); and his view that crops like cassava and maize spread widely only after 1880 and drove later growth. Colonial violence: scorched-earth in Maji Maji (1905-6) caused 'perhaps hundreds of thousands' of deaths mostly from starvation (up to half a million quoted).

Forced labour mortality: about 100 per thousand for Sao Tome contract labour (1915) and for the Brazzaville-sea railway (1922), 150 per thousand for the pre-1914 Cameroon railway; the Mossi proverb 'White Man's work eats people'; Free State concession system left population decline in the low-fertility belt, but Caldwell cautions the declines were exaggerated by high pre-partition estimates. Matches and tempers the course's Congo mortality caveats.

Health care under colonial rule: in 1939 medical budgets were two shillings a head in the Gold Coast and five pence in Nigeria; twelve hospitals served 4 000 Europeans in Nigeria while fifty-two served 40 million Africans; the doctor ratio was worse in 1939 than 1914. Chapter file stops at p. 479 of 486.

Caldwell's own estimates: Africa about 120 million in 1880 and 165 million in 1935 (his guess, not a count), the white population rose from about 750 000 to 3.75 million; 1918-19 influenza the highest annual death rate of the century; Rand mine death rates 71 per thousand for tropical Africans in 1907 (130 in 1905) and probably 200+ in compounds in 1913; urban growth in tropical Africa fivefold 1880-1930. Caldwell concludes colonial rule speeded up change but much would have happened anyway.

Afigbo argues African societies were never static and responses varied; boundaries fossilised and the Sokoto and Borno states lost territory while Samori's and Rabih's empires were split between colonies; the French broke up paramountcies while the British used rulers (exceptions: Morocco, Asante, Benin); colonialism turned racial distinctions into class divisions and created a literate new elite excluded from partnership, which led it into opposition. Useful for the course's Pan-Africanism and elite-formation material.

Religion as resistance and its limits: Maji Maji and Nyabingi (revolt in Kigezi 1928, cult suppressed 1934) crossed ethnic lines, Mwari cult in Rhodesia, Poro, war-charm movements in Madagascar and the Congo; Kenya's female-initiation controversy (missions banned it 1920-21, muthirigu song 1929, independent schools from 1923) fused with land grievance. Not in the course.

Islam and Christianity under colonial rule: Muslim share of Sierra Leone rose from 10% (1891) to 26.2% (1931); Sanusiyya led Libyan resistance 1911-32; Mahdism and Hamalliyya as anti-French movements; separatist churches (Tile 1884, Mokone 1892, Chilembwe 1915, Kamwana 1908, Kimbangu 1921, Harris 1910-15 with some 100 000 converts). Not in the course.

Opoku dates the Gusii Mumbo cult revolt to 1900, while Mwanzi in Chapter 7 and Chapter 8's East Africa tail date the Mumbo cult to 1913 (Onyango Dande). The two chapters disagree; 1913 is the better-supported date.

Arts under colonial rule: Soyinka argues art, music (mbira) and theatre survived and adapted; West African concert-party theatre from the 1900s (Bob Johnson; Ogunde formed during the period); Ecole William Ponty's staged cultural exercises from 1930; Egyptian press grew from 169 papers (1898) to 282 (1913). Cultural background only, with no direct fit in the course's lessons; kept as context for M3/M6 cultural-nationalism material.

Indigenous churches and the Musama Disco Christo Church (Gold Coast, founded 1919-22) as African Christianity on Akan lines; conclusion that colonial rule confirmed religious pluralism rather than destroying African religion. Context only.

League against Imperialism: the Comintern-sponsored Brussels Congress of 02/1927 had about 180 delegates and included Messali Hadj, Lamine Senghor, Jomo Kenyatta and South Africans J. T. Gumede and I. A. La Guma; Garvey's UNIA (launched 1917 in the US) reached colonies. Not in the M3 Pan-Africanism lessons.

Interwar nationalism: the state came before the nation; elites expected partnership after WWI and met frustration (van Vollenhoven 1917 warned of 'disillusionment, discontent and bitterness'); nationalism was not only urban and elite (protest migrations, deposition of chiefs, cocoa hold-ups, depression); settler colonies shaped tone (Devonshire declaration 1923 on Kenya); differing ideologies: assimilation in Algeria and Senegal, reform toward independence in British areas. Chapter 22's tail on the Comintern/Garvey sits in file ch-023, continued in ch-024.

Negritude: Soyinka dates its manifesto to Legitime Defense by Martinican students (c.1932), with Cesaire, Senghor and Damas as midwives, and treats it as a historical phenomenon that lost its hold as its circumstances disappeared. Fits the course's cultural-nationalism references.

Egypt 1919-35: Wafd formed 11/1918; Zaghlul arrested 8/3/1919 sparking the 1919 revolution across classes and faiths (Copts and women included); Milner mission, then Declaration of Independence 28/02/1922 with four Reserved Points (imperial communications, defence, minorities, Sudan); 1923 constitution gave the king power to dismiss governments; Fu'ad suspended it in 1924, 1928, 1930; 1936 treaty legalised British occupation. Not in the course.

Sudan 1919-35: White Flag League (1924, Ali Abd al-Latif) and Khartoum military revolt 27-28/11/1924; Nyala Mahdist revolt 26/09/1921; Aliab Dinka rising 30/10/1919, Prophet Ariendit, Nuer revolt 1927-8 with district commissioner Fergusson killed; neo-Mahdism of Abd al-Rahman built the Independence Front of the 1950s. Not in the course.

Interwar organisations (Gold Coast Youth Conference 1929, West African Students' Union, North African Star under Messali Hadj, Ligue universelle pour la defense de la race negre 1925); colonial governments cut humanities education (Ponty, Achimota, Makerere) to avoid India's example; 1935 Ethiopia invasion pushed pan-Africanism and negritude.

Maghrib interwar: Emir Khalid's election wins annulled and exile 1923; Jonnart Law 4/2/1919 (about half a million Muslim voters, Muslims limited to a third of town councils); Tunisian Destour founded 02/1920 (La Tunisie martyre); Etoile nord-africaine founded Paris 1924; Rif republic proclaimed 18/01 or 01/02/1923, Anwal 07/1921 (a 'reverse Omdurman'), Abdel Karim surrendered 26/05/1926; Ulema Association 1931; Algiers centenary 1930; Berber Dahir 16/05/1930 triggered over 120 incidents in three months. Not in the course (M4 l2 begins in 1945).

column4: ch-025 Chapter 24 (Berque), p. 613 and ch-002 Chapter 1, p. 3
column5: Ferhat Abbas's colonisation passage (a 'veritable revolution' for Algerians; first printed 1931, preface of 1930) appears both in Boahen's opening and in Berque; Abbas's early assimilationism (Le Jeune Algerien 1922-27) sits behind his later turn, useful for the M4 Algeria lesson's background.

Somaliland interwar: Italian annexation of Obbia 1925 and El Bur revolt (Italian Resident killed 15/11/1925); Sultan of Awsa; riots over western education at Burao 1922; Somali National League formed 1935; Osmaniya alphabet c.1920; Egyptian claim to Sudan shaped Wafd politics. Context for Horn of Africa; no course lesson.

National Congress of British West Africa: first conference Accra 11-29/03/1920, led by Casely Hayford and Akiwande Savage; 1920 delegation to London rejected (opposed by Clifford, Guggisberg, Ofori Atta, the Colonial Office); later sessions Freetown 1923, Bathurst 1925-26, Lagos 1930; Boahen argues it forced the elective-seat constitutions of Nigeria 1923, Sierra Leone 1924, Gold Coast 1925; leaders were co-operationist ('under the Union Jack'). Course M3 does not cover it.

West Africa interwar: 1919 Freetown riots and strike; Gold Coast Youth Conference 1929 (Danquah), Nigerian Youth Movement 1934 (Azikiwe, Awolowo), Wallace-Johnson's West African Youth League; Macaulay's NNDP 1923; unions illegal until 1932-41 (British) and 1937 (French); rural politics: Kwahu asafo 'Magna Carta' 1915-17, thirty-three chief depositions in Akyem Abuakwa 1910-44 and the 1932 asafo deposition of divisional chiefs and charges against Ofori Atta. Useful for M3 on pre-1945 nationalism.

Kenya roots of Mau Mau: Kikuyu Central Association from 1924 (Kang'ethe, Beauttah); Kenyatta general secretary 1928, edited Mwigwithania; KCA evidence to the Hilton Young Commission 1928 and the Kenya Land Commission 1932-33; 1925 petition against the 1915 Crown Lands Ordinance and for Thuku's release; author says the unmet land grievance led to the Mau Mau war two decades later. Missing from M2 Mau Mau background.

East African protest 1919-35: Ndonye wa Kauti's 1922 Kamba prophecy (taxes up from three to eight rupees by 1920, currency reform losses), Mumbo cult spoken revelation in 1913 to Onyango Dunde and about 150 Abagusii killed in 1914; Young Kavirondo Association (Lundha meeting 23/12/1921) tamed into the Kavirondo Taxpayers Welfare Association by Archdeacon Owen in 1923; Young Baganda Association 1919. This chapter dates Mumbo to 1913, supporting the earlier contradiction note.

Why British West African interwar nationalism had limited impact (no mass following, moderate methods, leader conflicts, elective seats 'anaesthetised' it, Casely Hayford died 1930); French West Africa: Diagne deputy 1914-34, Republican Socialist Party, diagnisme, High Commissioner for recruiting 1918; Paris groups (Houenou's Ligue 1924, Lamine Senghor, Kouyate); Porto Novo and Dahomey 1923 strikes and Hunkanrin's exile.

Bulhoek 1921: the chapter says soldiers killed 163 Israelites and wounded 129 (Enoch Mgijima's sect), where the course (from the TRC) says 183 killed. Bondelswarts 05/1922: about 100 killed and over 150 jailed, aircraft used (matches the course's 'about 100'). Check the TRC page for 183; do not state either figure without the source and flag the disagreement.

South African protest 1918-35: anti-dipping campaign 1913-17, women's trader boycotts Transkei 1922, independent churches (76 in 1918, 320 in 1932, 800+ by 1942), ANC took its name 1925 with Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika and a black-green-gold flag, Non-European Convention Kimberley 1926, All-African Convention Bloemfontein 12/1935; 1918 bucket strike (152 jailed) and 1920 strike of 71 000 African miners; ICU founded 01/1919 Cape Town, 30 000 members 1924, 100 000 in 1927 (Kadalie claimed 250 000); Communist Party of South Africa 1921, African majority by early 1930s. M5 checks the ANC name date correctly (1925).

Belgian Congo and Portuguese colonies 1919-35: Pende (Kwilu) rising 1931 with over 400 killed after prophet Matemu-a-Kenenia; Kimbangu arrested 14/09/1921, Kitawala under Tomo Nyirenda executed after 1926; Mbeni societies; Katanga strikes 1931-37 and the great 1941 strike; Portuguese forced-labour law of 1899-1914 lasting to 1961, assimilado status denied 99% of Africans; more than 100 000 northern Mozambicans had fled to Nyasaland by 1919; Angolan Liga Angolana dissolved 1922. Not in the course.

Liberia 1930-35: Christy League commission (report 08/09/1930) found forced recruitment and export of labour to Fernando Po with Frontier Force and official collusion, not organised slave trading; President King and Vice-President Yancy resigned 12/1930; Britain and US pressed for a Governing Commission 21/01/1931, Barclay refused; Brunot commission 1932; Firestone loan renegotiated 1935; US recognised Barclay 11/06/1935, Britain 16/12/1936. Akpan stresses colonial regimes were equally brutal. Not in the course.

Liberia and Ethiopia compared: Americo-Liberian oligarchy and Amhara-Tigrean dominance; Liberia a near one-party state with 1927 election count of 235 000 for King against at most 10 000 eligible voters; Ethiopia: Iyasu deposed 09/1916, Zawditu crowned 11/02/1917 with Tafari as regent, Tafari crowned Negus 07/10/1928 and Emperor 02/11/1930, 1931 constitution left absolute power; Ethiopia joined the League 23/09/1923; Firestone's 1926 lease of up to a million acres for 99 years.

Italian invasion of Ethiopia: Walwal 05/12/1934, invasion 03/10/1935 without a declaration of war, League vote 50 to 1 on 09/10/1935, limited sanctions (no oil), Hoare-Laval plan 07/12/1935 leaked and Hoare resigned 18/12/1935, Italians entered Addis Ababa 06/05/1936; International African Friends of Abyssinia formed 08/1935 with Kenyatta as secretary; Nkrumah's reaction quoted. Akpan explains Liberia survived while Ethiopia fell because Italy alone wanted to avenge Adwa.

column4: ch-030 Chapter 29 (Ralston), p. 772 vs ch-026 Chapter 25 (Boahen), p. 633
column5: Ralston says Casely Hayford used the impetus from Garveyism to found the NCBWA in 1917 (inaugural session Accra 03/1920), but Boahen's Chapter 25 attributes it to Casely Hayford and Akiwande Savage with the Garvey connection only a secondary influence; the volume's authors disagree on Garvey's weight. Treat Garvey influence as one input, not the cause.

Diaspora links: Garvey's UNIA (founded 1914) sent emissaries to Liberia 05/1920 and planned settlement of 20 000-30 000 families, technicians arrested and deported 1924, Liberia banned the UNIA; Negro World about 200 000 circulation, banned in Nyasaland by 1922, Kenyatta recalls Kenyans listening to it in 1921; Du Bois's Pan-African Congresses 1919, 1921, 1923; Washington's Tuskegee 1912 conference; African students in the US (Aggrey 1898, Azikiwe 1925-34, Banda, Nkrumah 1935) outnumbered black missionaries going the other way; Chilembwe studied in Virginia; Bulhoek leader Mgijima corresponded with Garvey. Compare M3 Garvey lessons.

Boahen's balance sheet: Gann, Duignan, Perham and Lloyd see a credit balance; Rodney a one-armed bandit; Boahen says positives were mostly accidental by-products. He cites Caldwell that Congo population halved in the first forty years of colonial rule, the Herero fell by four-fifths, the Nama by half and Libya lost 750 000, though Caldwell himself was cautious about population claims; colonialism ended the sovereign diplomacy of Asante, Ndebele and Madagascar in the 1890s.

Boahen states that in South Africa 89% of land was reserved for whites (21% of the population), 37% of Southern Rhodesia for 5.2%, 7% of Kenya for under 10% and 3% of Northern Rhodesia; these are later-period blends and conflict with Kaniki (Rhodesia 50.8% after 1930) and with the course's 7% for the 1913 South Africa Act. Boahen also calls land alienation the fundamental cause of Mau Mau. Use with care.

Economic balance sheet: no colonial government had an industry department before 1945; exports tied to one or two cash crops; food had to be imported (Gambia, Gold Coast, Egypt); crafts destroyed by cheap imports; urban growth (Nairobi 13 145 in 1927, Casablanca 2 026 in 1910 to 250 000 in 1936, Abidjan 800 in 1910); health and school gaps (12 hospitals for 4 000 Europeans vs 52 for 40 million Africans; Gold Coast about 80% of secondary schools in Cape Coast); only one university college per territory arrived after 1945; Swahili as lingua franca blocked by the Colonial Office. Chapter text stops at p. 802 of 809.

Kaniki's verdict: colonialism did bring some positive change but profits flowed to firms, banks and metropolitan reserves, while infrastructure was paid for by the colonies; 'growth without development'. Both the 'unmitigated disaster' and 'blessing' camps overstate. Fits the M1 balance-sheet lesson as one scholar's weighed judgement [CONTESTED between Rodney, Ajayi and Hopkins].

Colonial-era Europeans condemned African music, art, names and dress; baptism required a change of name. Newton (1923) and Coupland (1928) are cited as examples of the claim that Africa had no history. Useful for the lesson on the denial of African history.

Colonialism gave birth to African nationalism; power passed to the colonial-made elite, not to traditional rulers; the army and the borders (OAU sanctity of boundaries) are lasting legacies. Culture was 'additive', not 'substitutive', and rural life changed least; Kaniki puts the urban elite at about 20% [ESTIMATE]. Ajayi's 'episode' view versus Rodney's 'underdeveloped' view is a live debate [CONTESTED].
